name: Technological utopianism
summary: Technological utopianism holds that advances in science and technology can and should produce a utopia, with outcomes such as post-scarcity, transformed human nature and an end to suffering. Technology is seen as the main driver of social progress, its harms as manageable, and growth as the route to abundance. Politically it is a belief about means rather than a full programme, so its economic and social positions vary by strand.
scope: The mainstream contemporary strand: digital and Californian-ideology optimism, the 2023 Techno-Optimist Manifesto, and post-scarcity visions as described in Wikipedia's summaries of Gendron, Kelly, Gilder, Bostrom and Barbrook and Cameron. It leaves out the Marxist, Fabian and Soviet state-led variants, which would answer economic and state questions differently. Most answers outside technology, growth, regulation and energy are low-confidence inferences because the doctrine is a belief about technology, not a political programme.

sources.usedFor: Automation, abundance, work and money in post-scarcity visions and the split over ownership

universal-healthcare.rationale: Technological utopians split: statist and Marxist strands favour state provision, the Californian strand prefers markets and tech-driven cost cuts; no shared doctrine.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Productivity growth is said to lift wages on its own, but the tradition has no settled view on statutory wage floors.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The techno-optimist manifesto calls free markets the best way to organise a technological economy; statist strands dissent, so not +2.

public-ownership.rationale: The dominant Californian and techno-optimist strand favours private, competitive innovation, though Soviet-style variants made the state the engine of technology.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Californian ideology fused neoliberal economics with libertarianism, so higher taxes on wealthy entrepreneurs are unlikely to be favoured; inferred.

unions-good.rationale: The tradition says little on unions; knowledge-worker individualism leans against, labour-friendly socialist strands lean for.

property-fundamental.rationale: Libertarian digital strands stress property while Marxist and post-scarcity strands want it relaxed; the core doctrine is about technology, not property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The manifesto attacks regulatory capture, bureaucracy and the 'vetocracy' that it says block technological progress.

cut-welfare.rationale: The manifesto argues markets fund welfare and opposes UBI, but the core doctrine does not call for cutting welfare; adherents split.

worker-ownership.rationale: Post-scarcity writers discuss shared ownership of production, while market techno-optimists reject it; split along strands.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Digital utopians expected networked individuals to diminish state power and prize privacy tools; inferred, with little direct statement.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The counterculture half of the Californian ideology was drug-tolerant, the entrepreneurial half indifferent; no doctrinal position.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Digital utopians cast open networks as free expression and anti-state, so legal speech limits are disfavoured; inferred.

strong-leader.rationale: The manifesto praises dynamic markets and local knowledge over centralised decisions, which cuts against strongman rule; inferred.

state-harmful.rationale: Anti-statism is strong in the Western digital strands, but the tradition also includes state-led variants, and it does not call the state unnecessary.

limit-guns.rationale: No bearing on technological progress; adherents have no shared position.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; defence-technology enthusiasm and anti-state libertarianism pull in opposite directions.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: No doctrinal view; liberal-libertarian culture leans permissive but it is not part of the belief in technological progress.

decide-locally.rationale: The manifesto praises local knowledge over central decisions, but the doctrine is not federalist and supports global tech scale.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy is outside a doctrine about technology; surveillance and data tools could be argued either way, so adherents have no shared line.

traditional-family.rationale: The counterculture-influenced strands and visions of transformed human nature lean away from tradition-as-foundation; inferred.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Silicon Valley culture is socially liberal and technological utopians stress expanding personal freedom; inferred, not a doctrinal point.

abortion-legal.rationale: Same inference as for personal freedom: the culture is liberal on this, though the doctrine does not address it.

more-religion-public.rationale: Faith in science and technology as the route to utopia sits uneasily with a larger public religious role; inferred.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Critics link the Californian ideology to racial blindness while others stress inclusive access to tech; no doctrinal stance.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; adherents have no shared view.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The tradition prizes global progress and transformation over preservation of inherited customs; inferred.

gradual-change.rationale: The manifesto attacks institutions that block progress and gerontocracy, and e/acc wants speed; adherents reject deference to established institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Tech-optimists treat talent and growth as drivers of progress and oppose zero-sum thinking; inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Global-minded in outlook but wary of bureaucracy and vetocracy; no settled view.

free-trade.rationale: Free markets and abundance are central to the manifesto, but trade policy is not specifically stated; inferred.

nation-first.rationale: Progress is framed as universal and global, favouring cooperation; the manifesto does stress national technological strength, so only mild.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The sources discuss technology, not the use of force abroad; liberal interventionists and anti-war libertarians both appear among adherents.

open-borders.rationale: Pro-talent and pro-growth, but 'eventually open borders' is not a stated aim; adherents split.

limit-growth.rationale: The manifesto lists degrowth as an enemy and says lack of growth is a 'kill-all'; growth through technology is central.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Adherents want technology (nuclear, fusion) rather than restraint or drastic state mandates, and reject the precautionary approach.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: This is the definition of the ideology: technology is held to be the main driver of progress and to make problems manageable or end scarcity.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The manifesto calls fission a 'silver bullet' for clean energy and blames anti-nuclear rules for holding it back.

revolution-justified.rationale: Marxist strands endorse revolution; market and digital strands expect change through innovation. Genuinely split.

experts-over-public.rationale: The manifesto criticises the 'credentialed expert worldview' and favours local knowledge, though technocratic strands exist.

central-planning.rationale: The manifesto says central planning is doomed; the Soviet-style strand that disagrees is not the mainstream.

socialized-markets.rationale: Post-scarcity writers differ on whether markets survive under social ownership; no shared position.

land-value-tax.rationale: Taxation of land is never raised in the techno-utopian texts consulted, and no principle of the doctrine decides it.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Neoliberal and libertarian strands dominate; inferred, not stated.

basic-income.rationale: The manifesto explicitly opposes UBI, though automation-driven post-scarcity writers sometimes favour it; mainstream strand against.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Competition and open markets are held to drive progress; tariffs inferred as unwelcome.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Opposed to statism and central planning in the manifesto, though state-led tech variants (Soviet, North Korean) exist.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Market techno-optimists accept corporate scale while some digital-commons strands favour distributed ownership; the sources give no shared answer.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Post-scarcity writers imagine money fading in a world of abundance, but market techno-optimists reject this; split.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Not addressed; crypto-enthusiasts may agree, the rest are indifferent.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Corporatist price and wage setting conflicts with the market competition and anti-bureaucracy stance; inferred.

one-party-rule.rationale: Digital utopians expected technology to empower individuals and erode central power; Soviet-style variants are the exception.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Aristocratic legitimacy is at odds with the meritocratic and progress-oriented outlook; inferred.

democracy-best.rationale: Marx and others linked science with democracy and the manifesto praises liberal democracies; but the doctrine is not about regime form.

direct-votes.rationale: Early internet utopians hoped for direct digital democracy, but this is not a central or shared tenet.

workers-councils.rationale: Only the Marxist strand might favour it; the dominant strand rejects it.

right-to-secede.rationale: Network libertarians and 'exit' enthusiasts might agree; no doctrinal view.

natural-rulers.rationale: Belief in transforming human nature and democratising access conflicts with natural hierarchy; inferred.

political-violence-never.rationale: Marxist strands accept revolutionary violence while market and digital strands expect change by innovation; the doctrine is split rather than indifferent.

war-builds-character.rationale: The manifesto argues stagnation produces zero-sum conflict, and progress through abundance replaces struggle; inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: Secular, science-first outlook; inferred from the progress-via-science thesis.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Faith in technology and reason as drivers of progress makes scriptural law alien to the outlook; inferred.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Libertarian strand might accept; others reject; not a doctrinal point.

military-superiority.rationale: The manifesto ties free-world technological strength to defence, but this is not a core tenet.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Universalist progress and global networks stand against ethnic nationhood; inferred.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Marxist strand says yes, but the mainstream holds technology and growth, not class conflict, drive progress.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Market and growth framing stresses rising living standards for all, not equal outcomes; inferred.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Indigenous land rights are not discussed in the sources; nothing in the doctrine implies an answer.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations are not discussed in any consulted source, and growth-for-all optimism neither implies nor rules them out.

civilizational-union.rationale: Technological progress is presented as universal and networked rather than organised by religion or civilisation, so civilisational blocs are inferred as foreign to it.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Entrepreneurial ambition and competition are celebrated in the manifesto, a moral endorsement of striving; short of stating self-interest as moral.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Individual freedom and empowerment are stressed in digital utopian strands; inferred.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The manifesto says it believes in nature but also in overcoming it, treating nature's value as bound up with human flourishing.

limit-population.rationale: The manifesto lists depopulation among its enemies; adherents want more people and abundance.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Core claim is that technology is broadly positive and its problems manageable.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The manifesto calls for acceleration and e/acc pursues 'progress at all costs'; institutions are criticised as blocking it.

human-enhancement.rationale: The doctrine envisions transformed human nature and ending suffering and death; the manifesto champions augmented intelligence.

algorithmic-government.rationale: The manifesto treats AI as a universal problem solver, but it favours markets over state decisions; adherents split on government use.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The Californian strand's anti-state, individualist outlook favours private communication tools; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: The ideology looks forward to utopia through progress; restoring a lost order is the opposite orientation.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Technology-led pragmatism and 'what works' appeal, though adherents hold strong ideological faith in progress.

direct-action.rationale: Change is expected through innovation and markets, not protest; inferred.

means-match-ends.rationale: The prefigurative-politics question is not discussed; Marxist and market strands would answer differently.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Utterly opposed to the premise: technology is held to improve humanity's condition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Marx imagined this, but the mainstream techno-optimists see specialisation and productivity as drivers of abundance.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Post-scarcity writers imagine goods so cheap they are distributed freely, while market strands disagree.

production-for-use.rationale: Marx, Bookchin and Banks-style post-scarcity favour it; market techno-optimists favour profit-driven innovation.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The manifesto defends profit-driven competition as benefiting everyone; Marxist strand dissents.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Only the Marxist strand would accept it; the mainstream does not.

collective-farming.rationale: Soviet-era collectivisation is criticised in the manifesto (for example the Aral Sea); inferred.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The manifesto holds markets create abundance and reduce zero-sum conflict.

taxation-theft.rationale: Libertarian digital strand would agree; other strands would not; no doctrine.

harm-principle.rationale: The principle is liberal rather than technological; digital libertarians would accept it, state-led variants would not.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Digital libertarian strands stress individual rights while Soviet-style variants stress collective goals; no unified position.

conscription.rationale: The doctrine's emphasis on individual freedom and empowerment suggests aversion to compelled service, but it is not discussed; inferred.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Network libertarians favour exit, but this is not a doctrinal tenet.

state-as-business.rationale: The idea appears in some Silicon Valley circles, yet the consulted sources do not state it as a tenet.

positive-liberty.rationale: Technological abundance is said to expand freedom, but whether freedom requires state-backed material means is disputed between market and post-scarcity strands.

media-academia-power.rationale: The manifesto attacks credentialed experts and corroded institutions, but its claims about power are not this specific.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Hereditarian race theory conflicts with the doctrine's emphasis on universal progress and democratised access; inferred, not stated.

organic-representation.rationale: Corporatist representation by family and trade body is at odds with the network-individualist politics expected of digital utopians; inferred.

total-state.rationale: The manifesto rejects statism; digital strands expect technology to free individuals from big government.

national-rebirth.rationale: National decadence-and-rebirth narratives are not part of the texts; the manifesto's call for renewal through technology is not about the nation.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Expansion is framed technologically (space), not territorially; inferred.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal loyalty is the opposite of the modernising outlook; inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: Tying farmers to a lord is the opposite of the freedom and productivity that technological progress is credited with; inferred.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Science and technology are treated as objective drivers of progress; critics describe the view as scientism.

universal-morality.rationale: The sources are silent on moral epistemology; adherents range from rationalist universalists to relativists.

single-common-good.rationale: The manifesto's competitive pluralism of markets and local knowledge implies no single reasoned common good; inferred.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The question of a Jewish state is unrelated to technological utopianism and the sources give no view.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora citizenship rights are not addressed anywhere in the sources.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is not addressed by the doctrine.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; empowered knowledge workers appear in the tradition, but this is not codified.

school-vouchers.rationale: Market enthusiasm suggests sympathy but no consulted source states a position on education funding.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy is not discussed; Keynesian and austerity-minded adherents both exist.

economic-freedom.rationale: The Californian strand pairs the two, but other strands do not.

rule-by-example.rationale: Rule by moral example is a Confucian idea; the doctrine relies on institutions, markets and technology rather than ruler virtue, so inferred against.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; global-network optimism and national tech-strength themes pull in different directions.

force-without-un.rationale: The sources do not address the legality of force abroad.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith in rational science fits, but 'the only guide' overshoots what sources state, so mild.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Immigration and welfare eligibility are not discussed in the sources.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The manifesto opposes UBI but gives no stated view on work requirements; post-scarcity writers expect work to decline, so adherents split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Marxist strands reject it, market strands assume it; no shared position.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Institutions are called 'corroded' but the manifesto does not propose destroying libraries or museums.

dominated-front.rationale: A bloc against Western powers has no analogue in a doctrine that treats progress as universal and global; inferred.

workers-nation.rationale: Organising workers by nation is a nationalist-labour idea absent from a doctrine of technological universalism; inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The doctrine's emphasis on expanding personal freedom and ending constraints suggests rejecting legally fixed roles; inferred.

ban-interest.rationale: Prohibiting interest would disrupt the investment and financing on which the manifesto's market-driven innovation depends; inferred.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Legal racial separation contradicts the universal, democratising claims of technological progress; inferred.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Marxist strands call the state a class instrument while market strands do not; split.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Favours clean abundance via nuclear and solar, but the manifesto opposes restraint so only mild.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Cosmopolitan, talent-welcoming outlook makes compelled cultural assimilation unlikely to be endorsed; inferred, not stated.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy narrative with no place in the doctrine; inferred.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral-system design is not discussed in any consulted source.

national-mission.rationale: A national mission of exporting a government form is not part of the doctrine, which spreads technology rather than constitutions; inferred.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Structural gender analysis is not addressed; adherents range across ordinary political views.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The manifesto attacks regulatory capture and institutions, but no general claim about political elites.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Enhancement thought is about freedom and technology, not coercion; inferred.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Transitional-justice questions do not appear in the techno-utopian texts.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Libertarian digital strands endorse a minimal state, but statist variants of the tradition do not; split.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Discouraging mixing contradicts the doctrine's universalism; inferred.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Technology is said to democratise access; no explicit statement.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Concerns Marxist theory of socialist transition and is irrelevant to the market-leaning mainstream; no stance.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The sources do not take a position on settler colonialism.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Religious personal law is not discussed in the sources.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Restricting religious change conflicts with the individual-freedom orientation; inferred.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious-cultural ban is not part of the doctrine, and enthusiasm for new food technology points the other way; inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Secular, science-first orientation suggests support for schooling without religious instruction; inferred.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Marxist-Leninist logic about a strong socialist state is not held by the mainstream strand, which expects technology to erode central power.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Not stated, but the free-market and democratic lean implies it.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist export targets sit awkwardly with the manifesto's open competition among firms; inferred.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced removal of minorities is incompatible with the doctrine's universalism and individual freedom; inferred.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Libertarian digital strands endorse non-aggression, but other strands, including state-led ones, do not.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The manifesto calls competition the driver of evolution and innovation; applies it to markets, though 'peoples' overshoots.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The sources do not address militant democracy.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Republican freedom theory is not discussed; no position follows from the doctrine.

separated-powers.rationale: Constitutional separation of powers is not addressed in the sources.

vanguard-party.rationale: Only the Marxist-Leninist strand would endorse a vanguard party; the mainstream expects technology and markets, not a party, to drive change.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Growth and cheap goods are said to benefit everyone, but no priority principle.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: British housing policy is not addressed by the doctrine.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Industrial-relations law is not addressed in the sources.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The manifesto rejects depopulation thinking and says growth lifts people out of poverty.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Cosmopolitan networked outlook and talent-driven growth view suggest rejecting this claim; inferred.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Sortition runs against both electoral and meritocratic-market logic of the mainstream strand; inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The doctrine's liberty and anti-statist tendencies suggest opposition to suspending protections; inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The manifesto relies on market prices and abundance; inferred.

party-controls-media.rationale: Digital utopians hold networks free individuals from state control.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party control of the army belongs to Leninist systems, not the mainstream strand; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: A talent-welcoming, growth-oriented outlook suggests shorter, not longer, paths to citizenship; inferred.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay of legislators is not discussed in the sources.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The meritocratic, anti-gerontocracy tone of the manifesto and its stress on ambition over inherited standing suggest support; not stated directly.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Neither the tradition nor its counterculture and entrepreneurial halves take a common stance on state marriage.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A ban on renting is a heavy state intervention against market arrangements; the market-leaning mainstream would reject it, though the doctrine says nothing on housing.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The doctrine's sources do not address animals; enhancement-minded strands such as Bostrom's circle often care about suffering, others do not.

animal-use-humane.rationale: No source addresses animal use; alternative-protein enthusiasm and unconcern about farming coexist among adherents.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Territorial legitimacy is outside the doctrine's concerns and the sources give no view.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: The doctrine concerns technology and not constitutional founding values; adherents have no shared view.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Penalising religious exit is wholly contrary to the individual-freedom and rationalist outlook; inferred from the stress on personal liberty.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The expected route to utopia is innovation and markets, not insurgent vanguards; only strands of Marxist heritage might agree.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Foreign-policy tactics are not addressed; adherents divide along ordinary party lines.

ban-cartels.rationale: The manifesto says markets prevent monopolies through competition, but it also condemns regulatory capture; adherents split on antitrust.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Procedural constitutional matter the ideology does not address.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The manifesto holds that markets and technology continually raise productivity and create new work, so crises are survivable; Marxist strands dissent.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Open networks and personal freedom are central to digital utopianism, so moral censorship of art is rejected; inferred.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central banking is not addressed, though crypto-leaning adherents may dissent from the mainstream.

character-from-environment.rationale: The transformed-human-nature theme could point either way (environment or engineered biology); sources do not settle it.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is outside the doctrine; secular-science orientation implies indifference or mild opposition.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Cosmopolitan, talent-driven outlook favours a looser link of citizenship to ancestry; inferred.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Technology is expected to spread freely and empower individuals, not to justify rule over others; inferred.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist doctrine of party restoration of capitalism has no home in the mainstream techno-optimist strand.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule by religious scholars is opposed to the faith in science and technology as the route to progress; inferred.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Universalist and network-minded outlook does not endorse ethnic territorial claims; inferred.

collective-defense.rationale: The manifesto links free-world strength to technological strength but does not address alliances.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: A historical-legal question that the sources do not touch.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary integration is not addressed; some adherents like crypto or common standards, others prefer competition.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Constitution-writing procedure is not part of the doctrine.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The manifesto holds that infinite human wants drive jobs and growth and welcomes abundant cheap goods, rejecting the claim that more possessions do net harm.

corporate-influence.rationale: The manifesto condemns regulatory capture, which resembles this complaint, but also defends corporations as engines of innovation; adherents split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Digital libertarians favour limits on power and exit; the doctrine itself is silent, so mildly against.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Faith in science as the engine of progress makes teaching creationism as science contrary to the doctrine's premises.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Technological utopians typically rank societies by technological and material progress, but the sources do not say so outright.

death-penalty.rationale: Criminal-justice questions are not addressed by the doctrine.

defeat-communism.rationale: The manifesto condemns central planning and statism, but it does not call for defeating communism by confrontation.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A Leninist tactic with no counterpart in the mainstream strand.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Tribute-style hierarchical diplomacy has no place in this outlook, which looks to open networks and markets; inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Open markets, global competition and abundance are central; breaking ties would be contrary to the manifesto's claim that markets lift people from poverty.

democratic-peace.rationale: The manifesto links liberal democracies to technological strength and the abundance it says reduces zero-sum conflict; not stated as a thesis.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Constitutional design of the executive is not addressed.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Market-meritocratic strands tend to reject outcome-based tests; sources do not address.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources are silent on domestic violence policy.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic blocs contradict the open, competitive global market the manifesto champions.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The manifesto attacks the 'credentialed expert worldview' but also urges technical skill, so adherents are split.

elective-rulers.rationale: Market-and-meritocratic orientation and association of science with democracy imply election over inheritance; not a stated tenet.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Counterculture and entrepreneurial individualism prize unconventional living and heterodox thinking; inferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The manifesto links free-world strength to technology but does not take a position on alliances.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Meritocratic strands would favour abolition while others would not; the sources give no stance.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Constitutional entrenchment is outside the doctrine.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court policy is not addressed in the sources.

filial-duty.rationale: Traditionalist family duty sits poorly with a doctrine centred on transformation and individual freedom; inferred.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Neoliberal tendencies might favour it, but the manifesto proposes no tax design.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Not discussed; network libertarians sympathise with exit while state-led variants would not.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Open markets and global capital flow favour allowing foreign ownership; inferred.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Opposed to protectionism and state strategic planning; inferred.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Imperial nostalgia is not part of a progress-oriented outlook; inferred.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Libertarian digital strands might agree, but the doctrine itself takes no stand and other strands reject it.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Quotas conflict with a meritocratic, market-driven outlook; inferred.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Constitutional design of the executive is not addressed.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Universal progress narrative over civilisation-centred history; inferred.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Anti-colonial political economy is not addressed in the sources.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons policy is not discussed, although the manifesto is enthusiastic about civilian nuclear power.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Group-based political leadership clashes with the universalist, individual-empowerment outlook; inferred.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Market-friendly adherents may like private accounts but no source states it.

informal-organisation.rationale: Network-based, hierarchy-replacing structures are praised by digital utopians, but this is a statement about political struggle that the sources do not make.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The doctrine treats technology and open markets as universally beneficial; inferred against civilisational exceptionalism.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Military intervention to hold a bloc together is not part of the doctrine, and the libertarian-leaning mainstream opposes it; inferred.

job-guarantee.rationale: The manifesto expects technology to create new work on its own and trusts markets over state employment; inferred.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Ethnic-linguistic unification is foreign to the networked, universalist outlook; inferred.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Leninist theory of imperialist profits has no place in a doctrine that expects markets and technology to raise living standards broadly; inferred.

land-redistribution.rationale: Seizing estates is state intervention against property; inferred.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Property arrangements are not addressed; markets orientation implies against.

leader-cult.rationale: The doctrine's anti-hierarchy and empowerment themes oppose mass leader veneration; inferred.

local-production.rationale: The manifesto praises global markets and scaled technology; localism would be a form of the restraint it criticises.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The sources are silent on gendered social policy.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Digital utopians expected media to empower rather than pacify, but Frankfurt-style critique is not addressed.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The doctrine treats technology as a main driver of social change; Marx's productive-forces view is a named forerunner.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Inferred from the anti-statist, civilian-innovation outlook.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy theories about minorities have no place in a doctrine of rational, progress-through-technology optimism; inferred.

minority-veto.rationale: The manifesto's rejection of 'vetocracy' and calls to remove obstacles to progress conflict with veto rights.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-regime theory is not addressed.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: A market-friendly lean would accept, but the doctrine does not address service delivery.

moral-incentives.rationale: Rewards, ambition and competition are the drivers in the manifesto; moral incentives are the Maoist alternative.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural autonomy is not addressed by the sources.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Not discussed; global-minded outlook and wariness of bureaucracy conflict.

native-born-offices.rationale: Not addressed; meritocratic and cosmopolitan outlook suggests against.

no-bailouts.rationale: Market competition favours failure of firms, but adherents including large tech investors differ.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The sources do not address aristocratic duty; philanthropy by successful technologists is practised by some adherents but not doctrinal.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Libertarian digital strands sympathise but the doctrine does not state it.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Support for expanded personal freedom suggests agreement, but divorce law is not discussed; inferred.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial claims in peace deals are not addressed.

non-intervention.rationale: The sources are silent on non-intervention.

office-by-exam.rationale: Meritocratic spirit might attract, but experts are criticised in the manifesto.

paid-care-work.rationale: The sources do not address unpaid domestic labour, though automation-based abundance is sometimes said to remove such work.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Hierarchy-eroding, network-individualist outlook is at odds with binding party discipline; inferred.

party-own-road.rationale: Concerns communist parties only; not part of the mainstream.

patriotic-education.rationale: A universalist, progress-oriented outlook is cool toward school patriotism; inferred.

people-in-arms.rationale: The sources do not discuss military organisation.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The distinction concerns collectivist property models; the sources on post-scarcity note sentimental possessions persist but no stance is stated.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The sources do not discuss supranational integration.

precautionary-principle.rationale: The manifesto calls the precautionary principle 'deeply immoral' and demands it be jettisoned.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Culture-war monument debates are not addressed.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The manifesto lists depopulation among its enemies, favouring population growth, but state incentives are not addressed.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The sources give no general theory of property.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Digital utopians stress democratised access to knowledge and expression; this is a milder legal claim, inferred.

public-money-creation.rationale: Public control of money creation is not addressed and the market orientation suggests against; inferred.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall elections are not discussed in the sources.

refugee-return.rationale: The sources do not address refugee return.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The sources do not address regional autonomy within larger states.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The doctrine does not address exemptions from general laws.

religious-nation.rationale: Defining the nation by religion conflicts with the secular, universalist, science-first outlook; inferred.

residents-only-property.rationale: Restrictions on purchase limit markets, which the manifesto favours; inferred.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: The open, global orientation of the doctrine suggests opposition to such limits; inferred.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Western strands tie progress to freedom, though Soviet-style variants accepted authoritarian modernisation; mainstream dissent.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Digital-libertarian culture opposes content restriction; inferred.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentist claims are not addressed in the sources.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Abundance is expected to come from technology and markets, but aid is not addressed.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Minority strategy debates are not addressed.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony theory is not addressed.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The doctrine looks forward to technological civilisation and praises growth; pastoral moralism is the contrary view.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine kingship conflicts with the secular, progress-through-science outlook; inferred.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Market emphasis favours investment and trade over aid or autarky; not clearly stated.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The sources do not address curriculum on sex education.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical dispute outside the doctrine.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Opposed to unchecked state power per the anti-statism of the Western strands.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The sources do not address international debt.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate in Marxist theory; the sources do not take a position.

space-expansion.rationale: The manifesto says humanity's descendants will settle the stars; space expansion is a standard techno-utopian goal.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Church-state subordination is not addressed beyond a general secular lean.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The sources do not weigh in on this comparison, though the manifesto condemns central planning.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding standards on trade run against the anti-regulation outlook; inferred.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The doctrine pursues change through innovation rather than politics, but whether adherents should withdraw is not discussed.

women-must-cover.rationale: Compulsory dress is contrary to the individual-freedom outlook.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory conflicts with the manifesto's view that markets and technology lift everyone.

religion-illusion.rationale: Technology-driven abundance is expected to remove the hardships that sustain religion; inferred, though Californian optimists are split on religion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto praises markets and capitalism as engines of technological progress.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Strands split: post-scarcity thinkers see technology rather than economic change as the lever, while Marxist variants see systemic change; no doctrine.

socialized-care.rationale: Automation of domestic work is imagined, but whether as public service or private market products is split.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Technological utopians stress openness and innovation, with no concern for linguistic purity; inferred.

treaties-binding.rationale: The doctrine does not address internal-nation treaties; no basis for an inference.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Californian-ideology and manifesto strands favour markets and individual technological entrepreneurs, not commons; some post-scarcity writers differ.

majority-settlement.rationale: The doctrine is about technology rather than ethnic settlement; its globalist, market-minded strands would oppose steering it; inferred.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Post-scarcity visions and the Californian ideology both claim technology makes a new order beyond old capitalism or state socialism; inferred, contested.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The doctrine looks forward to abundance rather than backward to ancestral claims; inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not addressed; believers in rational progress and open knowledge are inferred to reject denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Californian and e/acc strands are liberal and pro-freedom on personal conduct; inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The manifesto and Californian strand favour open competition and free expression, and distrust centralised control.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Californian strand is libertarian-leaning and secular, so punishing speech is rejected; inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The doctrine favours markets and innovation over extraction; no documented position on colonies.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not addressed; the doctrine is secular and universalist, so the duty is inferred to be rejected.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Not addressed; the doctrine is secular, but removal by force is not part of it.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Strands split: some praise open networked participation, others favour market and founder-led decisions.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; the Californian strand is critiqued for ignoring racial and class structures.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Transhumanist and techno-optimist strands generally support individual self-determination; inferred.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred from its emphasis on ending suffering and expanding individual choice over life.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Barbrook and Cameron describe the Californian ideology as fusing counterculture left and libertarian right, and the manifesto claims ideas from both.

alienated-labor.rationale: Post-scarcity visions see automation freeing people from toil but strands split on whether capitalism or ownership is the problem.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The doctrine is universalist and secular; inferred.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The doctrine places hope in human ingenuity and technology, not in divine authority; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: No documented position; the libertarian strand opposes regulation while others favour it.

social-market-economy.rationale: The manifesto and Californian strand favour markets and technological growth with minimal regulation, not regulated social-market models.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The manifesto supports strong defence technology; abolition is inferred to be rejected.

rich-first.rationale: Accepts that innovators grow rich first as growth lifts everyone; inferred from the manifesto's growth and markets argument.

missingStatements.text: Governments should not slow the development of artificial intelligence.
missingStatements.rationale: The manifesto argues that slowing AI would cost lives because it is a universal problem solver.

missingStatements.text: Advances in technology can end material scarcity and with it most social conflict.
missingStatements.rationale: Gendron's thesis as summarised, and post-scarcity writers, expect abundance to eliminate major social evils.

notes: Strands diverge: Marxist, Fabian and Soviet variants favour state or collective ownership of technology, Californian and manifesto variants favour markets and anti-regulation. Answers follow the latter where they conflict, and use 0 for questions on which strands split.
